title: Manage plant manipulation methods of an agricultural crop

lessons.title: Planning a manipulation programme
lessons.html:
The manager's view

Plant manipulation, which includes pruning, training, thinning, canopy management, girdling, growth regulator use and pollination management, is one of the biggest levers on yield, fruit size, quality and timing in perennial and many annual crops. It is also labour intensive. Managing it means choosing the right methods for the crop and block, timing them correctly, resourcing them and checking results.

Setting objectives per block

Start from the block's history and goals:

  • Previous yields, fruit size distribution and pack-out percentages
  • Tree or vine vigour and canopy density
  • Alternate bearing tendency (common in some citrus, avocados and mangoes)
  • Market targets: size classes, colour, timing
  • Disease history, such as fungal problems in dense canopies

For example, a citrus block with small fruit and dense canopies may need heavier pruning to open the tree and more fruit thinning, while a vigorous young block may need training to build structure before cropping.

Choosing methods

ObjectivePossible manipulation
Increase fruit sizeFruit thinning (hand or chemical per registration), crop load management, girdling in some crops
Improve light and colourSummer pruning, deleafing, canopy opening, reflective mulch
Control vigourRootstock choice, summer pruning, root pruning, regulated deficit irrigation, growth regulators
Reduce diseasePruning for airflow, removing infected wood, skirting trees
Even budbreak after mild wintersRest-breaking agents in deciduous fruit, per label and adviser programme
Improve fruit setPollination units, pollinisers, bee management, growth regulators where registered

Timing and calendars

Build a manipulation calendar linked to phenological stages: dormancy, budbreak, flowering, fruit set, cell division, ripening and post-harvest. Many interventions have narrow windows; for example, thinning for size is most effective early, during cell division.

lessons.title: Resourcing, controlling and evaluating manipulation
lessons.html:
Resourcing the work

  • Labour planning: estimate hours per hectare per task from records; schedule teams so critical windows are met.
  • Skills: pruning and girdling need trained, experienced workers. Run training sessions with demonstration rows before each season.
  • Tools: sharp secateurs, loppers, saws, girdling knives, platforms and ladders, disinfectant for tools.
  • Chemical inputs: growth regulators, thinning agents and rest-breaking products must be registered for the crop and used strictly per label (Act 36 of 1947), applied by trained operators with PPE, and recorded.
  • Budget: manipulation costs per hectare compared with the expected improvement in pack-out and price.

Specifications and quality control

Write clear, measurable specifications per block, such as target fruit per tree, spacing between fruits, number of bearing shoots or canes, or girdle width. Supervisors sample trees per team and record compliance. Set an acceptable deviation; above it, rework and retrain.

Safety

  • Platforms and ladders inspected and used on stable ground.
  • Cut-resistant gloves where appropriate and safe knife handling for girdling.
  • Chainsaws and powered pruners only by trained operators with full PPE.
  • Heat stress management in summer work.

Evaluating results

  • Count fruit set and crop load after thinning.
  • Measure fruit size progression during the season against size curves.
  • Record yield, size distribution, colour, disease and pack-out per block.
  • Compare treated with untreated or differently treated rows where trials are run.
  • Calculate cost per hectare against the change in income.

Continuous improvement

After harvest, review each block with advisers and supervisors: what worked, what did not, and what to change next season. Keep block records over several seasons, since perennial crops respond over more than one year and alternate bearing can mask effects.

Key points

  • Set manipulation objectives per block from history and market targets.
  • Match methods to objectives: size, light, vigour, disease, budbreak, fruit set.
  • Time interventions to phenological stages; many have narrow windows.
  • Use trained teams, clear specifications and registered products per label.
  • Evaluate yield, size and pack-out against cost and review every season.
